A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same work and contain readable main text, equations, payoff tables, and Appendices A-C. Full-text comparison and visual inspection support a reliable assessment.

before.justification: v4 reports theoretical guarantees, analytical examples, and proofs. Neither the main text nor the appendices report original experimental, simulation, or data-analysis outcomes.

after.justification: v6 remains a theoretical paper. Its examples and appendix constructions are mathematical analyses, with no original empirical or simulation results.

M1.justification: Section 5.3 corrects the stated contract-design model: the agent's payoff becomes expected payment minus a nonnegative action-dependent cost c_a, in both payoff representations. The general learning framework, reduction, and Algorithm 1 remain unchanged.

E1.justification: Neither version evaluates datasets or empirical tasks. Bayesian persuasion, Stackelberg games, and contract design remain the same three theoretical applications.

E2.justification: The same learning classes and best-response benchmark are compared analytically. Neither version reports experimentally evaluated baselines; the additional citations do not introduce evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: Neither version reports experimental splits, evaluation metrics, training budgets, or testing protocols. The theoretical interaction procedure and feedback options are retained.

E4.justification: The mean-based-learning counterexample, approximate-response examples, and perturbation analyses are retained. No ablations, robustness experiments, or additional case analyses are introduced.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental run counts, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. Expectations and regret bounds remain theoretical quantities rather than empirical uncertainty estimates.

E6.justification: The quantitative utility bounds, illustrative payoff matrices, and qualitative findings are unchanged. Neither version contains empirical result entries, and apparent formula differences from extraction disappear when checked against the PDFs.

T1.justification: Section 5.3 revises both contract payoff definitions to subtract c_a and explicitly identifies their dependence on the decision variables as affine. The theorem statements, bounds, and mathematical content of Appendices A-C remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and discussion retain the same claims about the learning-to-approximate-response reduction, asymmetric utility bounds, and exploitability of mean-based learners.

C2.justification: Interpretations of the asymmetric bounds, cheap-talk equivalence, and learning-agent exploitability are retained. Section 6 already discusses the principal's environmental knowledge and extensions to unknown or non-stationary environments in v4.

D1.justification: Algorithm 1's pseudocode and the feedback descriptions are unchanged. No implementation settings, computational resources, or code/data access information are added or revised.

R1.justification: Sections 1 and 1.1 add Lin et al. (2023), Scheid et al. (2024), Harris et al. (2023), Lin and Li (2025), and Bacchiocchi et al. (2024). This modestly expands related-work coverage without changing the central positioning. Publication updates to existing references are not additional works.

P1.justification: Section 2.2 adds a paragraph making the principal's knowledge and expected-average-utility objective explicit. Other edits include localized wording changes, an ICLR acceptance footnote, and bibliography formatting updates; section and appendix organization are retained.

P2.justification: Text and bibliography reflow reposition existing displays: Example 4.1's payoff matrices move from page 16 to 17, and Algorithm 1 moves from page 24 to 25. Box formatting also changes slightly. No new figures or result tables appear.

improvement.justification: v6 improves the contract formulation by accounting explicitly for action costs in both payoff representations. The added explanation of the principal's knowledge and objective reduces ambiguity, while additional citations modestly improve research context. These are useful, limited refinements; the central theory and appendix proofs remain unchanged.
